title: Nearly-Optimal Bandit Learning in Stackelberg Games with Side Information
claim: Our bandit-based method nearly matches the optimal policy and keeps regret low, while the random baseline falls well short.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots; utility left, regret right; shaded confidence bands
description: Two side-by-side matplotlib line plots share the same x-axis, Time, from 0 to 200. The left panel plots cumulative utility for three methods: Optimal Policy in green, Algorithm1-OFUL in blue, and Random Baseline in orange. All three rise roughly linearly. Blue tracks just under green and orange falls clearly below both, with shaded variance bands around each line. The right panel plots regret for Algorithm1-OFUL and the Random Baseline. Orange regret climbs steadily to about 38. Blue regret flattens out at around 5 to 7, so it looks sublinear. Both panels have titles giving the setting (d=2, K=4, 4 leader actions, 4 follower actions) and a legend in the top corner. The eye goes first to the widening gap between the orange and blue curves on the right.
caption: Left: Cumulative utility of the optimal policy, [ref] instantiated with OFUL (Alg1-OFUL), and the random baseline over $T=200$ rounds in a setting with $4$ follower types, where each player has $4$ actions and the context dimension is also $2$. Right: Cumulative regret of Alg1-OFUL and the random baseline over $T=200$ rounds in the same setting. Results are averaged over $10$ runs.\looseness-1
abstract: We study the problem of online learning in Stackelberg games with side information between a leader and a sequence of followers. In every round the leader observes contextual information and commits to a mixed strategy, after which the follower best-responds. We provide learning algorithms for the leader which achieve $O(T^{1/2})$ regret under bandit feedback, an improvement from the previously best-known rates of $O(T^{2/3})$. Our algorithms rely on a reduction to linear contextual bandits in the utility space: In each round, a linear contextual bandit algorithm recommends a utility vector, which our algorithm inverts to determine the leader's mixed strategy. We extend our algorithms to the setting in which the leader's utility function is unknown, and also apply it to the problems of bidding in second-price auctions with side information and online Bayesian persuasion with public and private states. Finally, we observe that our algorithms empirically outperform previous results on numerical simulations.
